Raising the score: ca (number of coloured vessels) 1.11, a flat ST slope (slope:2) 1.04, asymptomatic chest pain (cp:4) 0.92, cholesterol 0.57, resting blood pressure 0.49, ST depression (oldpeak) 0.35, atypical angina (cp:2) 0.29, age 0.12. Lowering it: female sex (sex:0) -1.19, a normal resting ECG (restecg:0) -0.65, a normal thallium scan (thal:3) -0.61, a fixed thallium defect (thal:6) -0.53, typical angina (cp:1) -0.29. The weights of restecg:1 (0.09) and slope:3 (0.06) are small. In domain terms this part is a conventional risk score: the model gives men, patients with asymptomatic chest pain, a flat ST slope, more coloured vessels, higher cholesterol and blood pressure a higher predicted risk, and patients with a normal resting ECG or a normal thallium scan a lower one. One reading runs against clinical expectation: a fixed thallium defect lowers the score, so through this part the model ranks a fixed defect below a normal scan and both below a reversible defect (thal:7). This ordering rests on few patients: 15 training patients have a fixed defect, and the whole model still gives them a mean predicted risk of 65% (outcome rate 60%) through their other features. Self-probe: for the typical patient (a man aged 56 years with a normal scan), this part contributes -1.20 with a normal scan, -2.16 with a fixed defect and 0.03 with a reversible defect, and the whole-model predicted risk is 30%, 14% and 59%; switching the same patient to female moves this part from -1.20 to -3.71 and the predicted risk from 30% to 3%. This is the largest part: replacing every direct edge by its training-mean contribution lowers training AUC from 0.951 to 0.720. Age, ca, oldpeak and restecg:0 also feed hidden parts; their whole-model effects are given with the vessel brake and the normal-ECG gate.

Node 5364 rescales 3196 and adds a positive bias; both exits feed the output with positive weights. The formula is off by up to 0.0098 on the training rows from rounding. Nodes 2245, 7562 and 5364 are positive on 242, 242 and 242 of 242 training rows, so away from the brake the part is linear and rising in ca, a second vessel-count term on top of the direct ca edge. Hypothesis: the part adds risk as the number of coloured vessels rises, but a brake cuts that back for patients whose vessel count is high for their age. The brake is open on 17 training rows: 12 of the 12 patients with three coloured vessels and 5 of the 33 with two. This regime is fitted to 17 rows and runs against the data and clinical sense: those rows have an outcome rate of 82%, yet the brake lowers their score by 3.09 on average (switching node 5446 off changes their predicted risk by -0.094 on average, up to 0.59 in size, with minus without); most of them keep a high predicted risk (87% on average) because their direct terms are large. parts.name: cp3_offset
parts.original_hypothesis: 1173 ≈ relu(0.0489·cp:3 + 1.98) in z units, off by up to 0.0038 on the training rows from rounding the coefficients. The unit is positive on 242 of 242 training rows (share 1.00), so its ReLU does not bend on the data, and its value barely varies (sd 0.049 around a mean of 1.98). With its output weight of -1.41 it is mostly a constant shift of the score, i.e. part of the model's baseline. Its one varying input is non-anginal chest pain (cp:3), which it turns into a small reduction in predicted risk on top of the direct chest-pain edges. Self-probe: for the typical patient (a man aged 56 years), this part contributes -0.108 to the score with non-anginal pain against 0.044 with asymptomatic pain (relative to its training mean), so the model does lower the score for non-anginal pain through this unit, by a small amount. It matters little: replacing it by its training mean changes training AUC from 0.9508 to 0.9504 and flips 1 training prediction. This part is described rather than explained: it is a near-constant offset with a minor chest-pain term.

ann_31.text: Through this part, the model treats a higher number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy as raising the predicted risk of heart disease steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same: for a typical patient, it goes from about 30% at 0 vessels to about 84% at 2 vessels (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the resting ECG shows an ST-T wave abnormality (about 80%) than if the resting ECG is normal (about 30%) (on the training data only). The model has little data on this: only 2 training patients (an ST-T wave abnormality on the resting ECG).

Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise (about 77%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 30%) (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy (about 61%) than if the resting ECG is normal (about 30%) (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if thallium stress test result is something other than a normal thallium scan, a fixed defect on the thallium scan (about 59%) than if the thallium scan is normal (about 30%) (on the training data only).

Other effects: a higher serum cholesterol raises it steadily; typical angina (rather than no chest pain (asymptomatic)) lowers it; female (rather than male) lowers it; a higher resting blood pressure raises it steadily; non-anginal chest pain (rather than no chest pain (asymptomatic)) lowers it; a higher ST depression on exercise raises it steadily; atypical angina (rather than no chest pain (asymptomatic)) lowers it; a fixed defect on the thallium scan (rather than a normal thallium scan) lowers it; and 2 still smaller effects listed in the evidence table (on the training data only). The model has little data on some of these: only 15 training patients (a fixed defect on the thallium scan).

ann_32.text: Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a slightly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has non-anginal chest pain (about 27%) than if chest pain type is something other than non-anginal chest pain (about 30%) (on the training data only).

ann_33.text: This part acts on 86 of 242 training patients (36%); nearly all of them are patients with a normal resting ECG.
For a typical patient it acts on, it slightly raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 1% without this part to about 3% with it (on the training data only).
In the training data, 26 of these 86 patients had heart disease.

A higher maximum heart rate clearly lowers the predicted risk of heart disease, mainly if the resting ECG is normal (it also changes for 2 of the 121 training patients for whom it does not hold) (in an uneven way for patients with a normal resting ECG): for a typical patient, maximum heart rate going from 118 beats per minute to 175 beats per minute moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 65% to about 14% if the resting ECG is normal, and from about 21% to about 21% if resting ECG is something other than a normal resting ECG.

Other effects: ST depression on exercise past about 1.6 mm raises it with nothing until about 1.6 mm (between 1.6 and 3.8 mm for different patients), then steadily; a higher maximum heart rate lowers it in an uneven way; a higher ST depression on exercise raises it in an uneven way; ST depression on exercise depending on resting ECG raises it slowly at first, then faster; a higher number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy lowers it in a step, mainly the first vessel; any other resting ECG (rather than a normal resting ECG) lowers it; number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy past about 1 vessels lowers it in a step, mainly the first vessel; number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy depending on resting ECG raises it in an uneven way (on the training data only). The model has little data on some of these: only 19 training patients (of them, patients already past their fold).

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: maximum heart rate past about 92 beats per minute lowers it in an uneven way (on the training data only). The model has little data on some of these: only 11 training patients (patients whose resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy whose curve has a fold) and 1 training patients (of them, patients already past their fold).

ann_34.text: A higher number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if age is above 56 years (in a curve that is highest at about 2 vessels, lower either side for patients with age above 56 years): for a typical patient, number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy going from 0 vessels to 2 vessels moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 31% to about 94% if age is above 56 years, and from about 28% to about 76% if age is at or below 56 years.

Through this part, the number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy lowers the predicted risk of heart disease up to 3 vessels (for 183 of the 242 training patients it already changes above that): for a typical such patient, going from 0 vessels to 3 vessels moves it from about 15% to about 4% (on the training data only).

Through this part, the model treats a higher number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy as raising the predicted risk of heart disease in a curve that is highest at about 2 vessels, lower either side: for a typical patient, it goes from about 30% at 0 vessels to about 87% at 2 vessels (on the training data only).

Through this part, the model treats a higher age as slightly raising the predicted risk of heart disease with nothing until about 55 years, then steadily: for a typical patient, it goes from about 30% at 42 years to about 30% at 66 years (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise (about 77%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 30%) (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if thallium stress test result is something other than a normal thallium scan, a fixed defect on the thallium scan (about 59%) than if the thallium scan is normal (about 30%) (on the training data only).
